name: Pyritinol

card.summary: Vitamin B6 disulfide analog approved in several European countries for dementia-related impairment and sold as a US nootropic supplement; evidence is dated and mixed.
card.note: Rare severe reactions reported, including cholestatic hepatitis and pancreatitis; not FDA-recognized as a drug.

quick.overview:
Pyritinol is a semi-synthetic compound made by linking two vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) molecules with a disulfide bridge, produced by Merck in 1961. It is approved in several European countries for chronically impaired brain function in dementia syndromes and has been sold as a nootropic supplement in the US since the early 1990s.

Human trials are mostly old and small, with mixed results, and none addresses appearance.
quick.mechanism: Grokipedia (AI-generated) describes effects on brain glucose metabolism and cholinergic activity in animal and lab work. Wikipedia reports a half-life of about 2.5 hours.
quick.risks: Common effects are nausea and headache; mild skin allergy is rare. A 2004 survey of six case reports linked it to severe cholestatic hepatitis in patients on several drugs, and acute pancreatitis and a photoallergic eruption are also reported. Induced pemphigus has been reported in the dermatology literature.

lead: Pyritinol, also called pyrithioxine or pyridoxine disulfide, is a semi-synthetic water-soluble analog of vitamin B6 first produced by Merck in 1961.[1] From the 1970s it was sold as a prescription and over-the-counter drug in several countries, and since the early 1990s as a nootropic supplement in the United States.[1]

In several European countries it is approved for symptomatic treatment of chronically impaired brain function in dementia syndromes and for sequelae of head trauma; in France it is also approved for rheumatoid arthritis.[1]
infobox: Approved in several EU states; US supplement

paras: Approved indications in Austria, Germany, France, Italy, Portugal and Greece include dementia syndromes and craniocerebral trauma sequelae.[1]

A trial in 70 patients with probable Alzheimer's disease allocated them to social support, cognitive training, cognitive training plus pyritinol, or cognitive training plus phosphatidylserine for six months with neuropsychological, EEG and PET assessment.[2] A randomized study in cerebrovascular disorders examined vinpocetine and pyritinol together for blood rheology.[3] A 1973 double-blind trial compared pyritinol with placebo for preventing alcohol hangover symptoms.[4] Pharmaco-EEG studies have also characterised its effects on brain activity.[5] A 1993 European multicentre study compared it with auranofin in rheumatoid arthritis.[1]

Nausea and headache are common and mild skin allergy is rare; a 2004 survey of six case reports linked it to severe cholestatic hepatitis in patients on several other drugs, and acute pancreatitis and a photoallergic eruption are rare.[1] Pyritinol is among drugs reported to induce pemphigus.[6]

timeline.event: Sold as a nootropic supplement in the US.[1]
